body: SOUTH KOREA’S new president, Lee Jae-myung, faces an unenviable set of challenges as he takes office. One of the most pressing is addressing the persistent calls for South Korea to initiate a nuclear program. An increasing number of analysts — as well as some policymakers — in South Korea are now openly calling for either the development of nuclear weapons or at least for building nuclear latency.1 This interest is spurred by the growing nuclear threat from North Korea, China’s efforts to dominate the Yellow Sea, the mounting challenges facing South Korea’s existing deterrence strategy, and increasing uncertainty about US alliance credibility following the election of Donald Trump.

For South Korea, developing nuclear weapons systems that can survive an attack will be challenging, but not impossible. Even if mobile, South Korea’s ground-based missiles could prove vulnerable to a first strike. Its best option would therefore be to rely heavily on a sea-based nuclear capability.2 Its KSS-III submarines, which can fire ballistic missiles, would be a tremendous asset in a future nuclear weapons program. North Korea’s anti-submarine warfare capabilities are extremely limited, and South Korean submarines will therefore likely be highly survivable — if they are kept at sea. Keeping conventionally powered submarines on continuous deterrence patrols will be a significant strain for the South Korean navy, albeit one that it can likely handle given sufficient resources.

One option would be a strategy of pre-emption. With such a strategy, South Korea would rapidly strike against the North and try to neutralize its nuclear arsenal if it believed an attack was imminent. It could also opt for a launch-on-warning posture, where it would counterattack while North Korea’s missiles are in the air. While launch-on-warning would not prevent catastrophic damage to the same extent as pre-emption might, it could bolster deterrence.

In addition, it would need an advanced command-and-control infrastructure, and to keep its nuclear forces in a state of constant readiness. While South Korea is already developing many of these capabilities through its conventional deterrence strategy, a nuclear strategy based on pre-emption or launch-on-warning would be costly, create significant risks of mistakes and require perfect execution 100 percent of the time. Through such a step, South Korea would limit the risk that a strike against its leaders would leave its nuclear arsenal unusable. Delegated command-and-control arrangements come in various forms, and can certainly be matched with safety features, such as a “two-man” rule, where no single person is able to launch a nuclear weapon. An example of a pre-delegation procedure is the British “letters of last resort.”3 These letters instruct captains on ballistic missile submarines about what actions to take if a nuclear strike has destroyed the British government.

Moreover, implementing such procedures, including the selection of personnel and the provision of proper training in the handling of nuclear weapons, would be costly and time-consuming.

Even if they could address the decapitation challenge, South Koreans leaders would face another problem: North Korea’s tactical nuclear weapons. Kim Jong Un has said clearly that North Korea needs such weapons, and it has built a burgeoning arsenal of short- and medium-range missiles that can carry nuclear weapons.4

If war breaks out on the peninsula, North Korea could use tactical nuclear weapons at an early stage of the conflict. Anticipating losing or seeking to gain an early advantage, Kim Jong Un may attempt to force South Korea to back down with a limited nuclear strike — and threaten to inflict even greater pain with its remaining arsenal if South Korea fails to give up. Even if Kim does not use tactical nuclear weapons, he could threaten to. In other words, they provide North Korea with a powerful tool of coercion.

If South Korea decides to develop nuclear weapons, it must consider whether it needs tactical nuclear weapons of its own. In all likelihood, the demand for a “tit-for-tat” capability would be strong. If given time, South Korea could surely develop such weapons — but again, it would be expensive, operationally demanding and could exacerbate instability.

Although it is very challenging to assess breakout time, some experts claim that South Korea would need at least two to three years to develop nuclear weapons.​5 If Seoul acquires the reprocessing- or enrichment technology necessary to produce fissile materials, the breakout time could be reduced significantly — but weaponization could still take months, if not longer.

To be sure, there are steps South Korea could take to bolster deterrence even with a limited stockpile of warheads. Nevertheless, given the risks and challenges we have outlined, it is problematic to assume that the window of vulnerability will close the moment it has its first bomb in hand.
In addition, South Korean military planners may have to think beyond the problem of deterring North Korea.
An increasingly powerful and assertive China would present an even greater
military threat — for a nuclear South Korea
. Creating a nuclear arsenal that would be survivable in the face of China’s expanding conventional and nuclear might would be extremely demanding.

Proponents of the nuclear option may still argue that South Korea’s alternatives are even worse. Hoping for North Korean denuclearization has become a fool’s errand, and as noted, South Korea’s conventional deterrence strategy faces immense challenges. Relying on US extended deterrence — particularly given the uncertainty of Trump’s presidency — is also increasingly unpalatable for many. Nevertheless, the costs and risks of nuclearization for South Korea cannot be discounted. If its new leaders opt to build the bomb, they will face a series of hard choices — and their security could get worse before it gets better.
